Sally: Don't you wish we lived in a warmer climate? It's absolutely freezing today.
Peter: I wish I had gone to Africa. What a wasted opportunity!
Vanessa: With Amy? She asked you to go with her?
Peter: If she hadn't asked me to go, I wouldn't be so regretful.
Sally: At least that explains why you've been so down over the last week!
Vanessa: If you had gone, maybe you would have fallen in love.
Sally: Oh Peter. I wish you made better decisions when it comes to women. Hey, I know, why don't we take a trip of our own? We could go to the Caribbean! There are all-inclusive deals.

Vanessa: I wish I had the money, but I don't.
Peter: If I had told Amy how much I liked her, maybe it could have worked.
Sally: If you had gone, you also might have broken up, you might have been killed by a poisonous snake, you might have decided to never come back. The possibilities are limitless. There are so many things I wish I had done, but also so many things I'm glad I did. Maybe we should start thinking about the future. Like, don't you wish we could all take a trip together soon since it's cold outside?

Vanessa: I wish we were on the beach right now! I should have saved some money over the last year.
Peter: I wish I were kitesurfing on an aquamarine ocean with gentle waves. I wish I were lying under the blazing sun with a warm gentle breeze blowing.
Sally: That's the spirit!
Vanessa: If I hadn't paid so many bills this month, I would be the first to say we should go. Sorry to say, I am flat broke and on a strict budget for a while.

The Third Conditional - Talking Hypothetically About the Past

You use the third conditional to talk about unreal situations in the past.
These are things that did not happen in the past. You often use the third conditional to talk about regrets.
When you want to talk about situations in the past in a hypothetical context (not real or necessarily true), you can use the structures would have, should have and could have.
Look at the chart below for an outline of these structures within a third conditional sentence:
If I had told Amy how much I liked her, maybe it could have worked.
I should've saved some money over the last year.
If you had gone, maybe you would have fallen in love.

You use wish, plus the past form of the verb or the past participle of the verb to talk about imaginary situations in the past, present or future.

Wishes and sentences in the second and third conditional infer that what you want is probably not possible, or for some reason impossible and that you regret what happened in the past.

You use wish + Simple Past to talk about wishes in the present or future.
For example:
Sometimes I wish I had the money but I don't.
(I don't have the money.)

You use wish + could to talk about wishes for the future.
Example:
Don't you wish we could all take a trip together soon since it's so cold outside?

You use wish + had + past participle to talk about wishes about past situations.
For example:
I wish I had gone to Africa.
(I didn't go to Africa.)
